question.prompt: Suppose that \(n\) is the product of three consecutive integers and that \(n\) is divisible by \(7.\) Which of the following is not necessarily a divisor of \(n?\)

solutions.explanation:
Among any three consecutive integers, at least one is even and one is a multiple of \(3\). Their product is therefore divisible by both \(2\) and \(3\). It is also divisible by \(7\), as given. Since these are distinct primes, their product
\[
2\cdot3\cdot7=42
\]
divides \(n\). This conclusion also holds when \(n=0\), and negative products have the same positive divisors as their absolute values.

Each of \(6\), \(14\), \(21\), and \(42\) divides \(42\), so each necessarily divides \(n\).

However, \(28=2^2\cdot7\) requires two factors of \(2\). Consider the consecutive integers \(5,6,7\). Their product is
\[
210=2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7,
\]
which is divisible by \(7\) but lacks the second factor of \(2\) needed for divisibility by \(28\). Thus \(28\) is not necessarily a divisor, choice D.
solutions.title: Find the guaranteed factors
